paragraphs: The absurd distinctions of rank, which make civilization a curse by dividing the world between sensual tyrants and cunning, envious dependents, corrupt almost every class of people to the same degree. They do so because respectability is attached not to the carrying out of our duties to one another but to rank; and when the duties are not fulfilled, the affections cannot grow strong enough to fortify the virtue of which they are the natural reward. Still, there are some loopholes through which a man may creep out and dare to think and act for himself; but for a woman this is a Herculean task, because she has difficulties peculiar to her sex to overcome, which call for almost superhuman powers.

A truly benevolent legislator always tries to make it in each individual’s interest to be virtuous; and so, as private virtue becomes the cement of public happiness, an orderly whole is bound together by the tendency of all its parts toward a common centre. But the private or public virtue of women is highly doubtful; for Rousseau and a long list of male writers insist that a woman should be subjected all her life to a severe restraint, that of propriety. Why subject her to propriety — blind propriety — if she is capable of acting from a nobler motive, if she is an heir of immortality? Must sugar always be produced with living blood? Is one half of the human species, like the poor African slaves, to be subjected to prejudices that brutalize them, when principles would be a surer safeguard, merely to sweeten man’s cup? Is this not indirectly denying women reason? For a gift is a mockery if it is unfit for use.

Like men, women are made weak and self-indulgent by the enervating pleasures that wealth provides; but on top of this they are made slaves to their bodies, and must make them alluring, so that man may lend them his reason to guide their tottering steps aright. Or, if they are ambitious, they must govern their tyrants by underhand tricks, for without rights there can be no binding duties. The laws concerning woman, which I intend to discuss in a later part, make an absurd unit of a man and his wife; and then, by the easy step of regarding only him as responsible, she is reduced to a mere cipher.

The being who carries out the duties of its station is independent; and, speaking of women in general, their first duty is to themselves as rational creatures, and the next in importance, as citizens, is that of a mother, which includes so many others. The rank in life that excuses them from fulfilling this duty necessarily degrades them by making them mere dolls. Or, if they turn to something more important than simply fitting clothes onto a smooth block, their minds are occupied only by some soft platonic attachment, or the actual conduct of an intrigue may keep their thoughts in motion. For when they neglect their domestic duties, it is not in their power to take the field and march and counter-march like soldiers, or to wrangle in the senate, to keep their faculties from rusting.

I know that, as proof of the inferiority of the sex, Rousseau has triumphantly exclaimed, How can they leave the nursery for the camp! And some moralists have called the camp the school of the most heroic virtues; though I think it would puzzle a sharp casuist to prove that most of the wars that have dubbed men heroes were reasonable. I do not intend to examine this question critically, because I have often regarded these freaks of ambition as the first natural stage of civilization, when the ground must be torn up and the woods cleared by fire and sword, and so I do not choose to call them plagues. But surely the present system of war has little connection with virtue of any kind, being a school of FINESSE and effeminacy rather than of fortitude.

Yet suppose that defensive war, which is the only justifiable war in the present advanced state of society, a state in which virtue can show its face and ripen amid the hardships that purify the air on a mountain top, were alone accepted as just and glorious: then the true heroism of the ancients might once again stir the hearts of women. But gently and softly, dear reader, male or female, do not be alarmed. Although I have set the character of a modern soldier beside that of a civilized woman, I am not going to advise women to turn their distaffs into muskets, though I sincerely wish to see the bayonet beaten into a pruning hook. I was only refreshing an imagination wearied by dwelling on the vices and follies which all spring from a foul stream of wealth that has muddied the clear brooks of natural affection. I did so by supposing that society will one day be so constituted that man must fulfil the duties of a citizen or be despised, and that while he was employed in any branch of civil life, his wife, also an active citizen, would be just as intent on managing her household, educating her children and helping her neighbours.

But to make her truly virtuous and useful, she must not, if she carries out her civil duties, lack the protection of civil laws in her own right. She must not depend on her husband’s bounty for her living during his life, or for her support after his death — for how can a being be generous who has nothing of its own? Or virtuous, who is not free? As things now stand, the wife who is faithful to her husband but neither nurses nor educates her children scarcely deserves the name of a wife, and has no right to that of a citizen. But take away natural rights, and of course duties come to an end.

So women inevitably become nothing more than the wanton amusement of men, when they are so weak in mind and body that they cannot exert themselves except to pursue some frothy pleasure or invent some frivolous fashion. What sight could be more melancholy to a thinking mind than to look into the many carriages that drive helter-skelter about this city in the morning, full of pale-faced creatures who are running away from themselves? I have often wished, with Dr. Johnson, to put some of them in a little shop, with half a dozen children looking up to their languid faces for support. I am much mistaken if some hidden vigour would not soon bring health and spirit to their eyes; and some lines, drawn by the exercise of reason on those blank cheeks, which before had been rippled only by dimples, might restore lost dignity to their character, or rather enable it to reach the true dignity of its nature. Virtue cannot be acquired even by speculation, and still less by the passive idleness that wealth naturally breeds.

Besides, when poverty is more disgraceful than even vice, is morality not cut to the quick? Still, to avoid being misunderstood: although I consider that women in the ordinary walks of life are called by religion and reason to fulfil the duties of wives and mothers, I cannot help lamenting that women of a higher class have no road open by which they can pursue wider plans of usefulness and independence. I may provoke laughter by dropping a hint, which I intend to follow up at some future time; for I really think that women ought to have representatives, instead of being governed arbitrarily without being allowed any direct share in the deliberations of government.

But since the entire system of representation in this country is at present merely a convenient handle for despotism, women need not complain; they are as well represented as a large class of hard-working artisans, who pay for the upkeep of royalty when they can barely stop their children’s mouths with bread. In what sense are those people represented whose very sweat keeps up the splendid stables of an heir apparent, or varnishes the carriage of some royal mistress who looks down on shame? Taxes on the barest necessities of life allow an endless tribe of idle princes and princesses to parade in stupid pomp before a gaping crowd, who almost worship the very show that costs them so dear. This is mere Gothic grandeur, rather like the barbarous and useless display of mounted sentries at Whitehall, which I have never been able to see without a mixture of contempt and indignation.

How strangely corrupted the mind must be when it is impressed by this sort of pomp! But until these monuments of folly are levelled by virtue, similar follies will leaven the whole mass. For the same character will, to some degree, prevail throughout society as a whole; and the refinements of luxury, or the vicious grumbling of envious poverty, will alike banish virtue from society as its defining characteristic, or allow it to appear only as one of the stripes in the harlequin coat worn by civilized man.
